text:
Citation:

Dhami et al v.
Southam Inc. et al

Date:

20020409

2002 BCSC 464

Docket:

C993413

Registry:  Vancouver

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

BETWEEN:

MANJIT SINGH DHAMI

HARJIT SINGH ATWAL

PIARA SINGH NATT and

JAGTAR SINGH SANDHU

PLAINTIFFS

AND:

SOUTHAM INC.

and KIM BOLAN

DEFENDANTS

REASONS FOR JUDGMENT

OF THE

HONOURABLE MR. JUSTICE CLANCY

Counsel for the Plaintiffs:

E.
Rice, Q.C.

Counsel for the Defendants:

B.T.
Gibson, Q.C.

Date and Place of Trial:

Vancouver,
B.C.

January
28-30, 2002

February
4, 2002

[
1
]

Southam Inc. (“Southam”) is the publisher of the
Vancouver Sun newspaper (the “Sun”).  Kim Bolan is a reporter employed by that
paper.  The plaintiffs bring this action alleging that they were defamed by
Southam and Ms. Bolan.  They say that Ms. Bolan falsely and maliciously wrote
and Southam published an article in the Sun on May 15, 1999.  The article
is said to contain defamatory statements which would be understood to mean that
the plaintiffs threatened to kill and then killed, or had others kill, one Tara
Singh Hayer.  They allege that their reputations “have been brought into public
scandal, odium and contempt …”.  They seek general, special, aggravated and
punitive damages, interest, special costs and an injunction restraining Southam
and Ms. Bolan, or others on their behalf, from publishing any similar libel.

Facts

[
2
]

Mr. Hayer was a controversial newspaper
publisher in the Lower Mainland of British Columbia.  He published and wrote
for the Indo-Canadian Times.  He was killed in November 1998.  No charges have
ever been laid in connection with his death.

[
3
]

Prior to Mr. Hayer’s death, on March 6, 1998,
the plaintiffs brought an action against him, the Indo-Canadian Times, the
Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (the “CBC”), their reporter and other
defendants.  The endorsement on the writ of summons claimed damages for
defamation arising from a CBC broadcast entitled "Broadcast One:  Beyond
Table and Chairs”.  Some of the defendants named in that action allegedly made defamatory
statements when interviewed during the broadcast.  Although Mr. Hayer and his
newspaper were named as defendants in the writ, no claims were advanced against
them.

[
4
]

After the death of Mr. Hayer, the writ of
summons was amended on March 3, 1999, to add a claim against Indo-Canadian
Times International Inc. and Indo-Canadian Times for damages for defamation for
republishing defamatory statements made in the broadcast.

[
5
]

On learning of the defamation action and the
allegations made against Mr. Hayer and his newspaper, Ms. Bolan wrote the
impugned article.  She mistakenly believed that the action had been brought on
March 3, 1999.

[
6
]

The headline above the article was, “Slain
publisher being sued for libel”.  The subheading read, “Militant opponents of
Tara Singh Hayer, the moderate Sikh who was shot dead last November, are suing
him for defamation over an article he published in his Indo-Canadian Times in
March 1997”.

[
7
]

The article contained the following paragraphs:

A group of long-time
fundamentalist opponents of slain newspaper publisher Tara Singh Hayer have
launched a libel suit against him even though he was assassinated last
November,
The Vancouver Sun
has learned.

Piara Singh Natt,
Jagtar Singh Sandhu, Harjit Singh Atwal and Manjit Singh Dhami, all linked to
the militant International Sikh Youth Federation, outlined their claim against
Hayer and his
Indo-Canadian Times
in a writ filed in March.

The four are suing
Hayer for defamation over an article he published in March 1997, based on a
CBC-TV report about the finances at Surrey’s Guru Nanak temple when it was
controlled by the ISYF.  The suit also names the CBC.

…

Hayer’s daughter
Rupinder, who has taken over the paper, says the suit is just part of the
on-going campaign of some Sikh extremists who have tried to bankrupt the paper
by filing numerous suits over the years.

“They knew how
costly it was.  It was one way of trying to stop him,” Rupinder Hayer said.

[
8
]

The article then went on to describe how a
search of court records showed that Mr. Hayer, or his paper, had been named in
12 lawsuits since 1990.  Ms. Bolan specifically referred to actions filed by
Talwinder Singh Parmar and Ripudaman Singh Malik.  Mr. Parmar was described as
the Babbar Khalsa leader and the number one suspect in the 1985 Air India bombing.
Mr. Malik, who has subsequently been charged in connection with the Air India
bombing, was described as a controversial Khalsa school president.  Ms. Bolan
went on to say that other actions among the 12 were filed by Mr. Hayer’s
competition in the Indo-Canadian media, members of the International Sikh Youth
Federation (the “ISYF”) and the newspaper of the ISYF, the Charhdi Kala.  She
described how Mr. Hayer had brought six lawsuits of his own and the fact that
he had succeeded in an action against Charhdi Kala and several defendants,
including Mr. Sandhu and Mr. Atwal, two of the four plaintiffs in this action.

[
9
]

Ms. Bolan then referred to Charhdi Kala as
having been sued eight times and to other actions brought against other
Indo-Canadian publications.  She noted that most of the suits were eventually
dropped or dismissed and then quoted Mr. Hayer’s daughter, Rupinder Hayer, as
stating that the real objective was to cost Mr. Hayer as much money as
possible.  Ms. Hayer was quoted as saying:

They were always trying to tie him up in the
courts….  When that didn’t work he was threatened.  And when that didn’t work,
he was killed.

[
10
]

On May 27, 1999, the plaintiffs, through their solicitor, wrote to
the solicitors for the defendants.  The letter states:

The article generally casts the late Mr. Hayer
as a “moderate” besieged ruthlessly by “militant opponents” including our
clients whom you expressly identify as part of the latter group.  The headline
states:

“Militant opponents
of Tara Singh Hayer, a moderate Sikh who was shot dead last November are suing
him for defamation…”

Most disturbing to our clients, however, are
the words quoted of Rupinder Hayer:

“They were always
trying to tie him up in the Courts,” she said of her father.  “When that didn’t
work, he was threatened.  And when that didn’t work he was killed.”

The unmistakable and outrageous implication of
those words is that our clients killed Mr. Hayer or caused him to be killed.

[
11
]

A full apology was demanded on behalf of the plaintiffs.  By letter
of June 1, 1999, the Sun’s solicitors replied:

The Vancouver Sun understood Ms. Hayer’s
comments to refer to militants in general, rather than to your specific
clients.  The Vancouver Sun also believes that the ordinary reader would
understand those comments to refer to militants in general.  We do not
therefore believe that your clients have been defamed.

[
12
]

Both defendants have refused to apologize.

History

[
13
]

There are deep divisions within the Sikh community in British
Columbia.  Some understanding of the sources of friction are necessary so that
the impugned article can be considered in its proper context.  The following
summary is based on evidence given at trial by the litigants.  It may or may
not be historically accurate but both sides in this dispute appear to share an
understanding that the divisions within the Sikh community arose in the manner
described.

[
14
]

Under British rule in the Indian subcontinent there were three main
communities, the Hindus, the Muslims and the Sikhs.  The Muslims were
successful in obtaining their own community when Pakistan was created.  The
Hindu population was dominant in India.  Both Pakistan and India wished to have
the Sikhs remain with them and, according to the evidence, the Sikh leaders
were concerned over losing their identity if they joined either, on a formal
basis.  They did, however, decide to remain part of India.

[
15
]

In 1947, the British left and the Indian parliament passed a new
constitution.  No provision was made in the constitution for the protection of
Sikh culture.  As a result, a feeling grew within the Sikh community that they
should have their own homeland.  Sikhs demanded that a Sikh state, based on the
Punjabi language, be formed in the north of India, in the Punjab.  After a
period of unrest during which many thousands of Sikhs were jailed, the Punjab
was created within India.  By 1982, more local autonomy was demanded.  Unrest
followed and in 1984 Indian government troops stormed the Golden Temple, the
holiest site to those of the Sikh faith.  In the years following the storming
of the Golden Temple support grew for the creation of an independent Sikh state
to be called Khalistan.

[
16
]

Many Sikhs in the Lower Mainland supported the idea of Sikh
independence and, during the 1980s, a division developed within the Sikh community
over the issue.  In his writings, Mr. Hayer at first supported the formation of
a separate state and the cause of separation.  Later, he reversed his position
and withdrew his editorial support from the separatist cause.

[
17
]

A second source of friction within the community arose during the
1990s.  Within the Sikh religion there is a belief in a higher authority.  A
priest referred to as “Jathadar” occupies an office similar to that of the Pope
in the Catholic faith.  With him are five other priests.  Those priests issue
edicts to Sikhs throughout the world.  In 1999 they issued an edict that all
adherents to the faith should sit on the floor in the temple and refuse to use
tables and chairs.  In the Lower Mainland some Sikhs refused to obey, while
others followed the higher authority.  Whether obedience to the higher
authority is required of Sikhs became a volatile issue within the community.

[
18
]

Generally speaking, the faction which supports the creation of
Khalistan and whose members follow the dictates of Jathadar refer to themselves
as orthodox or traditional Sikhs.  The English language press, including the
Sun, refers to them as fundamentalists.  Sikhs who do not accept traditionalist
positions on religious and political matters are referred to in the press as
moderates.  For ease of reference, I will refer to the factions as
traditionalists and moderates in these reasons.

[
19
]

Prior to his death in November 1988, Mr. Hayer was involved in two
other incidents.  At one time a bomb was found either in or near his premises
and then, early in 1988, he was shot and left partially paralyzed during an
assassination attempt.

[
20
]

All of the plaintiffs deny any involvement with the bomb, the
wounding of Mr. Hayer and his death.  They further deny any knowledge of who
may have been involved and state that they have never spoken publicly in favour
of the killing of Mr. Hayer.  They testified that the Sikh religion opposes the
taking of human life.

[
21
]

As many as 200,000 Sikhs reside in the Lower Mainland area.  There
are three places of worship - the Ross Street Temple, the Guru Nanak Temple and
the Dasmesh Temple.  The Dasmesh Temple was established in 1998 by
traditionalist Sikhs.  Prior to its establishment, the traditionalists and
moderates both tried to obtain control of the Ross Street Temple and the Guru
Nanak Temple.  Ross Street came under control of the moderates, and when
moderates then gained control of the Guru Nanak Temple, the traditionalists
formed a new congregation at the Dasmesh Temple.

[
22
]

In Ms. Bolan’s article, reference is made to the ISYF.  That body
was formed to preach Sikhism to youth and to persuade Sikhs that they should
have a homeland in India to be called Khalistan.  From the evidence it is clear
that the ISYF is widely regarded by the English language press as a militant
and extremist Sikh federation, passionately espousing the formation of
Khalistan.  It has been described as a terrorist organization by both Canadian
and U.S. officials.  I need not decide whether that description is justified.
It is sufficient to say that is how it has been described by the media.

[
23
]

A brief history of Ms. Bolan’s coverage of the Indo-Canadian
community for the Sun provides further context.  She has reported on the
community since 1984.  She has written many, many articles, particularly about
the divisions within the Sikh community.  The policy of the Sun, followed by
her, is to refer to traditionalists as fundamentalists and to the
non-traditionalists as moderates.  At trial, she agreed that she refers to
traditionalists as militants but never applies that term to moderates.
Previous articles written by her have associated the ISYF with violent actions,
including murder.

[
24
]

Ms. Bolan has linked the traditionalists to the ISYF and other
extremist groups, including Babbar Khalsa, a group identified in the article as
having been led by Talwinder Singh Parmar.  Ms. Bolan was familiar with Mr.
Parmar and said that he supported the armed struggle for Khalistan.  She said
Babbar Khalsa was connected to Akhand Kirtani Jatha (“AKJ”), a separatist group
with which Mr. Malik was involved.

[
25
]

Ms. Bolan has written favourably of the activities of Mr. Hayer.
She became his personal friend, a fact which was widely known.

[
26
]

A number of her articles were produced at trial to establish
context.  I have read the articles carefully and find that a clear pattern
emerges which links the traditionalists to groups that advocate an armed
struggle for Khalistan and whose members are widely considered to be prone to
violence.

[
27
]

All of the plaintiffs testified to being devout Sikhs.  In many
ways, and in different degrees, the lives of all four revolve around religious
activities.  Each was involved in an official capacity with the Guru Nanak
Temple.  All broke away and now attend Dasmesh Temple.

[
28
]

All have admitted links in the past to the ISYF.  It is fair to say
that all have been shown to be militant traditionalists.  The evidence of Ms.
Bolan makes it clear that the traditionalists have been linked to groups prone
to violence.

[
29
]

There is no evidence linking any of the plaintiffs to the killing of
Mr. Hayer; however, all have been shown to be his opponents.  Despite the
protestations of some, I find that all have been shown to have had an active
dislike of him and, in some instances, have published their views.  Two of them
were successfully sued by Mr. Hayer.  That fact would have been well known in
the Sikh community.  The plaintiffs were by no means the only opponents of Mr.
Hayer.  The evidence establishes that there were many others who did not share
his views.

[
30
]

Ms. Bolan reviewed the wide publicity given to the death of Mr.
Hayer.  She said that several theories had been advanced in various articles in
the press.  In those articles the police were quoted as stating they were
investigating Mr. Hayer’s opponents.  His family was quoted as saying that Sikh
extremists were responsible.

[
31
]

As to the article of May 15, 1999, she felt that her reference to
lawsuits was even handed.  As to the article of May 15, 1999, Ms. Bolan
confirmed that the statements attributed to Rupinder Hayer are accurate.  She
understood that Ms. Hayer’s reference to “they” was to her father’s opponents,
the fundamentalists.

[
32
]

She said that she does not apply the terms “extremists” and
“militants” to moderates, only to traditionalists.  She agreed that she has
linked the ISYF to violence, including murder.

The Issues

[
33
]

Two questions arise from the pleadings.  The first is whether Ms.
Bolan’s article of May 15, 1999, defamed the plaintiffs.  With reference to
that question, it is important to remember that it is only the defamation
pleaded that concerns the court.

[
34
]

The second issue arises only if the article is defamatory.  It may
be stated as:  Did the article damage the reputation of the plaintiffs?

Did Ms. Bolan’s Article Defame the Plaintiffs?

[
35
]

I recognize that it may be that multiple plaintiffs will not always
succeed or fail together.  Here, the evidence of all four plaintiffs is so
similar that I will consider them as a group.  On the question of liability, I
can see no basis for treating any of the plaintiffs separately.

[
36
]

Manjit Singh Dhami’s complaint concerns his co-workers at
International Forest Products Ltd.  They showed him an article and asked, “Did
you guys do this?”  His daughter, who is a law student, asked him the same
question.  In both cases he denied the suggestion but said he felt degraded and
became depressed, ashamed and reluctant to go to work.  He was unable to sleep
for a few days.  He added that remarks were made referring to him as a
terrorist and that a copy of the article was hung in the lunchroom.  On
examination for discovery, Mr. Dhami was unable to name anyone who had spoken
to him.  At trial, he supplied the name of one person but that person was not
called as a witness.

[
37
]

In 1990 and 1991 Mr. Dhami was General Secretary of Guru Nanak
Temple.  He became President in 1992 and 1993.  He was involved in the
formation of Dasmesh Temple and has been General Secretary of that temple for
two years.

[
38
]

Mr. Dhami claims for damages for loss of income.  He sells insurance
in his off hours and has done so since 1997 or 1998.  His complaint is that the
article ruined his reputation, making it difficult for him to go to people to
meet their insurance needs.

[
39
]

Harjit Singh Atwal was a realtor.  He said that he was affected by
the Bolan article.  His son and people with whom he was dealing asked him about
it.  It was hard for him to face those people.  They asked why his name was in
the paper but never asked him directly if he was involved.  Instead, they asked
why his name was there if he was not involved.  That, he said, made him feel
bad.

[
40
]

Mr. Atwal gave the names of persons who spoke to him about the Sun
article and who asked him why his name was in the paper.  In response to those
inquiries, he stated that he had nothing to do with the death of Mr. Hayer.
One person advised him that people would read the article and think that he was
involved.  On Examination for Discovery, he had agreed that all that person had
said was “Your name is in the paper.”  At trial, Mr. Atwal said that was true
but again repeated that the person had said that others would assume he was
involved.  None of the witnesses were called to support Mr. Atwal’s
recollection.  His complaint about the article was that it was hard for him to
face those people.

[
41
]

Although Mr. Atwal stated that he had lost real estate commission
income to such an extent that he left the real estate business in the year
2000, he adduced no evidence concerning his loss.

[
42
]

Piara Singh Natt’s daughter asked him if he was involved in the
murder after she saw the article.  He denied it.  On reading the article, he
felt he was falsely accused, and after discussing the article with family
members he decided to take the matter to court.

[
43
]

People asked him what “his story” was, and people at the temple
asked why the story was in the paper if he was not involved.  He said he could
not go to the temple for a few weeks because he could not concentrate on his
prayers.

[
44
]

He was uncertain whether he had lost any business.  There was no
evidence of loss adduced.

[
45
]

Mr. Sandhu described how he had suffered as a result of the May 15,
1999 article.  He felt he had built up his character over 20 years and that the
article had given him a bad name.  He said he was very upset.  Other people and
his children asked him about the article and would not believe his denials.  He
said his insurance business suffered.  People stopped coming to him.  He claims
a loss of approximately $10,000.

[
46
]

Ms. Bolan confirmed that a Mr. Bagga pleaded guilty to the charge of
attempting to murder Mr. Hayer.  He was quoted by the police as stating that
people involved with Babbar Khalsa and the ISYF had helped him, although
apparently that admission was later denied.  Publicity was given to the fact
that he had stayed with an ISYF member and that he had written articles for
Chardhi Kala.

[
47
]

Ms. Bolan agreed that both she and Southam had refused to
apologize.  She felt that the article was clear and would not be understood by
an average reader to identify the plaintiffs as the persons who threatened to
kill and were involved in the killing of Mr. Hayer.

[
48
]

Much evidence was led on matters such as allegations of past
misconduct of the plaintiffs and allegations of bias on the part of Ms. Bolan.
The specifics of misconduct of the plaintiffs goes only to reputation.  It is
not relevant to the question of whether or not they were defamed.  Ms. Bolan’s
alleged bias is of no evidentiary value.  The question is whether the articles
she wrote defamed the plaintiffs.  I will not deal with the additional
evidence.

Discussion

[
49
]

The plaintiffs appended the May 15, 1999 article to their statement
of claim as Schedule “A”.  The specific pleading of the plaintiffs which
alleges libel is found in paragraph 9 of the statement of claim.  It reads as
follows:

The statements contained in Schedule “A” are
defamatory in the natural and ordinary meaning and in the innuendos contained
therein in that they mean and were understood to mean that the Plaintiffs
threatened to kill and then killed or had others kill Tara Singh Hayer.

[
50
]

In paragraph 10 the plaintiffs go on to claim that they have been
severely injured in their “credit, character and reputations as citizens and
have been brought into public scandal, odium and contempt, and have suffered
loss and damage.”  They plead that the defamation was motivated by actual or
express malice, in that the defendants failed to properly investigate the
underlying facts and ignored information which tended to disprove the
allegations.  They deny that the defendants held an honest belief that the
defendants had threatened to kill, or had others kill, Mr. Hayer.

[
51
]

The defendants deny the allegations in the statement of claim and
specifically deny that the words of Schedule “A” “in their natural and ordinary
meaning or by innuendo, bear the meaning set out in paragraph 9 of the
statement of claim.”

[
52
]

In his careful argument, Mr. Rice agreed that an allegation
referring to a large group to which the plaintiffs belong is not actionable.
He contended, however, that the ordinary meaning of the words used and the innuendo
implicit in those words is that the plaintiffs threatened to kill Mr. Hayer,
did kill him, or had someone else kill him.

[
53
]

The law is stated in R.E. Brown,
The Law of Defamation in Canada
,
2d ed., vol. 1 (Toronto: Carswell, 1994) at p. 299:

The test in every case is whether the ordinary
sensible person to whom the words were published would understand them as
referring to the plaintiff.

[
54
]

The court is entitled to look at the story itself, as well as the
general context in which the words would be read:  R.E. Brown,
The Law of
Defamation in Canada
, 1
st
ed., vol. 1 (Toronto: Carswell, 1987)
at pp. 140-141.

[
55
]

Mr. Rice referred to Brown,
supra,
2d ed. at pp. 200-302:

It is not necessary
that the plaintiff be identified by his or her proper name, or even mentioned
at all, if it is otherwise shown that the words would be reasonably understood
to refer to the plaintiff. …  The question in such a case is whether or not the
words used are such as to lead an ordinary sensible person, or reasonable
persons, who pay reasonable attention to the contents of the communication, to
understand that it was the plaintiff to whom the defendant referred.

…

In determining whether it is the plaintiff to
whom the defamatory remarks point, the court may take into consideration the publication
as a whole, the identity of the speaker, the context and circumstances in which
the publication was made, the mode by which it was conveyed, the occasion on
which it occurred, and the audience to which it was directed.  The ordinary
sensible reader is not expected to read or listen to the publication with the
precision of a lawyer, and he or she can be expected occasionally to indulge in
a certain amount of loose thinking and draw some far-fetched inferences.

[
56
]

It is argued that the plaintiffs are clearly implicated in the
killing of Mr. Hayer because the article identifies them as militant
fundamentalist opponents of Mr. Hayer.  The plaintiffs say further that the
reference to the libel suit, being part of the “ongoing campaign of some Sikh
extremists who have tried to bankrupt the paper by filing numerous suits over
the years”, implies that the plaintiffs would be involved in that ongoing
campaign.  They say that the plaintiffs’ libel action against Mr. Hayer would
obviously be included among the 12 lawsuits mentioned.

[
57
]

The defendants contend that since the libel suit against Mr. Hayer
was brought by the plaintiffs after his death it could not possibly be included
in the actions which were brought to tie up Mr. Hayer in the courts.  That
contention cannot be accepted.  The action brought by the plaintiffs was, in
fact, brought before Mr. Hayer’s death.  Ms. Hayer’s reference to tying Mr.
Hayer up in the courts would necessarily include actions against the
Indo-Canadian Times.  Her words, when read in context, would indicate to an
ordinary reader that the plaintiffs’ libel suit was part of the campaign
referred to by Ms. Hayer.

[
58
]

Armed with those conclusions, the plaintiffs refer to the quoted
words of Rupinder Hayer, who said that the persons bringing the action were
trying to tie up her father in the courts and “when that didn’t work he was
threatened, and when that didn’t work, he was killed.”  The plaintiffs contend
that the natural inference is that “they”, with reference to tying Mr. Hayer up
in the courts, referred to the 12 lawsuits and included the plaintiffs, and
further that “they” were responsible for threatening and killing Mr. Hayer.

[
59
]

In the article Ms. Bolan also referred to a Mr. Rampuri, who had
initially opposed Mr. Hayer but later reconciled with him.  She said he “was
one of the first to condemn his assassination, which many believe occurred
because Hayer refused to be deterred from writing against extremism.”  The
plaintiffs say that reference also links Mr. Hayer’s death with extremism and
therefore with the plaintiffs.

[
60
]

Finally, the plaintiffs contend that the implication that they are
involved in the death of Mr. Hayer is enhanced by various descriptions of them
found within the article, including the fact that they were militant opponents
of Mr. Hayer, that they were linked to the militant ISYF, that they launched
their libel suit against Mr. Hayer after he was killed and that Mr. Natt had
been convicted of smashing tables and chairs.

[
61
]

It was common ground that some readers of the Sun would be casual
readers, unfamiliar with the issues, while others may have followed the
articles written by Ms. Bolan over a period of years and still others would be
members of both factions within the Sikh community, familiar with the issues.

[
62
]

An ordinary reader must therefore include casual readers, followers
of articles written by Ms. Bolan and other reporters in the Sun, members of the
moderate Sikh faction and members of the traditionalist faction.

[
63
]

I disagree with the plaintiffs’ contention that an ordinary reader
would understand that they are clearly named as being involved in the killing
of Mr. Hayer.  The article does not make that allegation, nor is it suggested
by innuendo.  I find that an ordinary reader, whether a casual reader, a
follower of Ms. Bolan’s articles or a member of one of the Sikh factions, would
understand that the plaintiffs had brought an action against Mr. Hayer for
defamation, that they were fundamentalist or traditionalist Sikhs, that they
were opponents of Mr. Hayer and that all four were linked to the militant
ISYF.

[
64
]

The ordinary reader would also understand that the action brought
was part of a campaign of some Sikh extremists to bankrupt Mr. Hayer’s
newspaper.  The further inference the reader would draw is that the campaign
had failed, after which Mr. Hayer was threatened and then killed.

[
65
]

Rather than identifying the plaintiffs as those persons involved in
the killing of Mr. Hayer, an ordinary reader would conclude that the plaintiffs
are identified in the article as members of two groups: (1) a group of
litigants who were attempting to bankrupt the newspaper, some of whose members
threatened and killed Mr. Hayer and (2) traditionalists having ties to
extremist Sikhs who had committed acts of violence.

[
66
]

A casual reader might not understand that the ISYF was alleged to be
an extremist organization but followers of the coverage by the Sun and members
of both sides of the Sikh community would know that the Sun had labelled the
ISYF as an extremist organization, prone to violence.

[
67
]

The law pertaining to actions involving persons who are members of
groups is succinctly set out in Brown,
supra
, 2d ed. at pp. 324-327 as
follows:

The general rule is that an attack on a
substantially large and indeterminate group of persons does not give rise to a
cause of action to any of its members, unless there is something in the
publication pointing to a particular member, or making it susceptible of
special application to an individual in a class.

…

Where, however, a libel is directed against the
whole of a relatively small class of persons, the finger of condemnation may
point to every member.

…

Where the group is relatively small, and the
statement refers to the group or all members of the group, the persons defamed
as ascertainable, and each person within the group may have an action for
defamation.  For the same reason, if the plaintiff plays a very prominent role
in the group, it is more likely that he or she would be singled out.

However, it must first be established that the
plaintiff belongs to the class to which the defamatory remarks were directed,
and that the words had some personal application to him or her.  While the size
of the group is probative, the true test in determining whether the plaintiff
has been referred to is the “intensity of the suspicion cast upon the
plaintiff” by the defamatory publication.

[
68
]

I have found that there is nothing in the article specifically
naming the plaintiffs as the particular members of the larger group of Sikh
extremists who threatened and killed Mr. Hayer.  Neither does a reasonable
interpretation of the article lead to that conclusion.  As to their
identification as members of a group of Sikh militants or extremists, I find
that the evidence shows that Sikh extremists are a large and indeterminate group
of persons.  In the absence of language having some personal application, its
individual members have no cause of action.  The words used here do not have
personal application.  The action cannot succeed on the basis that the
plaintiffs were identified as extremists.

[
69
]

As to the group of litigants, the plaintiffs are not identified
directly, nor by innuendo, as the particular litigants who threatened and
murdered Mr. Hayer.  The action cannot succeed if it is based on that
contention.

[
70
]

It does not matter whether certain people might read the story in
the manner suggested by the plaintiffs:
Dale’s Trad’n Post Ltd. et al v.
Rhodes and Southam Inc.
(1987),
1987 CanLII 2475 (BC SC)
, 19 B.C.L.R. (2d) 73 (S.C.), citing
Halprin
v. Sun Publishing Company Ltd. et al
,
1978 CanLII 2564 (BC SC)
, [1978] 4 W.W.R. 685 (B.C.S.C.).
Similarly, a story that casts suspicion in the direction of the plaintiffs is
not sufficient:
Booth v. B.C.T.V. Broadcasting System
(1982),

1982 CanLII 251 (BC CA)
, 139 D.L.R. (3d) 88 (B.C.C.A.).  In
Butler v. Southam Inc.
(2001),

2001 NSCA 121 (CanLII)
, 197 N.S.R. (2d) 97 at para.
74
(C.A.), the Court held:

As noted earlier, the fact that the articles
could raise some immediate suspicion that the appellants did the things alleged
is not, of itself, sufficient to ground liability.

[
71
]

The question then becomes whether the described group of litigants
who brought actions against Mr. Hayer is sufficiently small, such that each
member may have had a cause of action or that the plaintiffs had a prominent
role within the group.

[
72
]

There is a reference to 12 actions having been brought.  It is at
least arguable that a group of 12 litigants is sufficiently small as to make
the accusation against them actionable.  An ordinary reader would, however,
understand that actions are not necessarily brought on behalf of one person.  I
was not provided with the pleadings in all of the actions but a review of some
of the writs that were issued shows that multiple plaintiffs were involved in
some of the actions.  In all, there were 20 plaintiffs involved in the eight
actions reviewed.  Some plaintiffs have corporate identity.  For example, in
Action C955075 thirteen plaintiffs are named.  They include the Guru Nanak Sikh
Gurdwara Society which would appear to have numerous members.  Given the number
of plaintiffs and the need to include within the group of litigants members of
the Society, or at least a majority of them, the group is much too large to
seriously argue that all of those persons were involved in the threatening and
murder of Mr. Hayer.

[
73
]

I find that the group of litigants named is not sufficiently small
so that all members could have claimed that they had been defamed.  The
authorities on which the plaintiffs relied are of no assistance to them.  They
related to discrete groups such as a jury, a committee, commissioned merchants
and a group of Jewish persons in Montreal:  see
MacKay et al. v. Southam
Co. Ltd. et al.
(1955),
1955 CanLII 286 (BC CA)
, 1 D.L.R. (2d) 1
(B.C.C.A.);
Masters et al. v. Fox et al.
(1978),
1978 CanLII 2057 (BC SC)
, 85 D.L.R. (3d)
64 (B.C.S.C.);
Ortenberg v. Plamondon
(1914), Q.O.R.
24 K.B. 69
(Que. K.B.)
.

[
74
]

I agree with the defendants that both the group of extremists and
the smaller group of litigants are too large to allow the plaintiffs to bring
an action on the basis that they were identified as members of either group.
Additionally, neither group of litigants is sufficiently well defined to allow
a conclusion that each member of it has an action in defamation.  It is
impossible to state which members of either group are alleged in the article to
be those who killed Mr. Hayer.  An ordinary reader would conclude that not all
extremists nor all litigants were involved.  By way of support for that
conclusion, I note that there is also reference in the article to a Punjabi
poet, Gurcharan Rampuri.  He is named as a person who commenced a libel suit
against Mr. Hayer but the article goes on to state that he later reconciled
with him and was one of the first to condemn his assassination.  It seems
improbable that he could claim that he had been defamed by the article.

If the Article is Defamatory, Did the Plaintiffs Suffer a
Loss of Reputation?

[
75
]

At trial, the plaintiffs complained of references in the article
which they found to be offensive but which were not related to the threatening
and killing of Mr. Hayer.  The pleadings make no claim in respect of those
words.  The law provides that the law of defamation protects a person’s
reputation.  In considering the admissibility of evidence in Brown,
supra
,
2d ed. at p. 1536, the author states:

To determine the
reputation held by the plaintiff, the parties may call those familiar with him
or her and ask them to give evidence with regard to that part of the
plaintiff’s reputation made relevant by the nature of the defamatory remark.

[
76
]

In P.L. Lewis,
Gatley on Libel in Slander,
8
th
ed.
(London: Sweet & Maxwell, 1981) at para. 1348, the authors discuss whether
other defamatory words about which the plaintiff has not sued are admissible to
show animus.  They state:

… the jury should be cautioned against giving
any damages in respect of it.  And if such evidence is offered merely for the
purpose of obtaining damages for such other injury, it will be properly
rejected.

[
77
]

Here, the defamation complained of is that the statements contained
in the article, in their ordinary meaning or by innuendo, mean that the
plaintiffs threatened to kill and then killed or had others kill Tara Singh
Hayer.

[
78
]

The references in the article to extremism, militants, Mr. Natt’s
prior involvement with the tables and chairs dispute and the naming of the
plaintiffs as litigants who sued Mr. Hayer in order to bankrupt him are not
relevant to the allegation that they killed or were involved in the killing of
Mr. Hayer unless those comments, combined with the statements of Rupinder Hayer
imply that the plaintiffs were the litigants or extremists who were involved in
Mr. Hayer’s death.  For the reasons already given, I have concluded that an
ordinary reader of whatever description would not draw that conclusion.  The
descriptions may be offensive to the plaintiffs, but they are not related to
the killing of Mr. Hayer and therefore are not relevant to the defamation
pleaded, nor are those descriptions relevant to the question of whether the
plaintiffs have suffered a loss of reputation.

[
79
]

I have decided that Ms. Bolan’s article did not defame the
plaintiffs.  Given that conclusion, I do not propose to deal further with loss
of reputation other than to say that if my conclusion is wrong, I would add
that the evidence of loss of reputation was highly unsatisfactory.  The only
evidence of a loss of reputation came from the plaintiffs themselves.  There is
no doubt that an allegation of the kind complained of would diminish the
reputation of virtually anyone.  The plaintiffs’ links to violent extremism and
the evidence of allegations of past misconduct of at least some of them would,
however, have the effect of reducing any award for damages.  Any award I might
have given would not have been substantial.

Malice

[
80
]

As to malice, although it was pleaded, it was not argued.  I
conclude, in any event, that the evidence does not support the allegation of
malice.  Ms. Bolan may favour the moderates but there is no evidence of malice,
nor do the statements in the article support the plaintiffs’ allegation.

Conclusions

[
81
]

I conclude that the claim of the plaintiffs must fail.  Ms. Bolan’s
article is critical of Sikh fundamentalists and extremists, as are previous
articles published in the Sun.  The ordinary reader would not, however, find
that the plaintiffs were identified in the article as being involved in the
killing of Mr. Hayer.  I need not therefore deal with the evidence of loss of
reputation.

[
82
]

Similarly, I will not consider the claims for special damages. The
issue does not arise.  The evidence on the issue was, in any event, highly
unsatisfactory.  Mr. Atwal and Mr. Natt did not allege any loss.  Mr. Dhami and
Mr. Sandhu failed to show, on a balance of probabilities, that they suffered
any monetary loss.

[
83
]

The action is dismissed.  The defendants are entitled to their costs
on Scale 3.

“D.L.
Clancy, J.”

The Honourable Mr. Justice D.L. Clancy
